overview: Chenla is a Chinese historical name associated with powerful early Khmer centers, including Ishanapura in present-day Cambodia. Scholars debate how united these polities were. The atlas’s 600 to 900 span and broad outlines are schematic: identical early polygons cannot prove stable borders, and the ninth-century outline overlaps the emergence of Angkorian power.

periods.title: Ishanapura and early royal power
periods.summary: Isanavarman’s court and substantial brick temples made Ishanapura a major seventh-century center.

periods.title: Regional rulers and temple communities
periods.summary: Inscriptions document local patrons and dependent communities; the extent of political unity remains debated.

periods.title: Transition toward Angkor
periods.summary: New Angkorian royal centers emerged, while earlier sacred places continued to be used and altered.

items.text: Chinese histories describe Chenla’s rulers, cities and military expansion. Local inscriptions name officials, settlements and royal conquests. Reading them together reveals organized political power, but royal boasts and a foreign writer’s categories cannot supply exact borders for every year. Historians still disagree over the scale and structure of these early states.

A Sanskrit inscription dated to 627 tells how Isanavarman appointed Vidyavisesha to royal duties and later made him governor of Tamandarapura. The same text records a religious foundation supported by a village with fields, gardens, cattle, buffalo and servants. Officeholding, worship and agricultural resources were closely connected.

Vidyavisesha’s inscription praises his command of grammar and philosophical systems and calls him a poet. It also says he cherished his friends. The polished praise offers a glimpse of an educated official’s ideals: intellectual skill and loyal relationships belonged alongside political service. It does not tell us that every child attended school.

Sambor Prei Kuk’s builders combined brick sanctuaries, selected sandstone details and foundations or supporting structures made from local laterite. Some shrines have eight sides. Their forms connect with South Asian architecture, but Khmer craftspeople developed a distinctive local style whose influence continued into the Angkor period.

Some temple walls carry carved images of flying palaces. These heavenly buildings belong to religious imagery, not a record of ancient aircraft. The miniature architecture lets us see how craftspeople made a brick wall suggest a much larger sacred world. A palace could soar in the imagination while the real building stayed firmly on the ground.

The temple zone was part of a larger landscape of watercourses, ponds and raised routes. UNESCO records causeways connecting the sacred area toward the river and a possible harbor. Building and maintaining these features required coordinated work. Their presence demonstrates water management, without proving that every household had piped water or a toilet.

The seventh-century Trapeang Prey inscription assigns white rice to support people living at a temple. It also lists cattle and buffalo among donated resources. Sacred establishments needed recurring supplies and human work: impressive worship still depended on getting food to people.

The same record lists women together with their children among people given to temple service. The older translation calls them slaves. These family lists preserve individuals otherwise difficult to see, but they also expose coercion and inequality behind religious endowments.

Excavators at the city’s M.90 terrace recovered fragments of bowls, jars, spouted vessels and clay stoves. The site was used over a long period, so every piece cannot be assigned to one reign. Pottery helps reconstruct storing, pouring and preparing food, although fragments in construction fill cannot reveal one family’s dinner.

The Old Khmer inscription K.127 includes śaka parigraha 604, meaning “Saka year 604.” This is a scholarly Roman transliteration, not the stone’s original letter shapes. The current edition reads 604 where older publications read 605, placing the record around 682 or 683 CE. Even a single weathered numeral can change a historical date.

K.127’s date uses a zero as a placeholder. That tiny mark matters because it lets a numeral distinguish six hundred and four from sixty-four. It is an important early Cambodian witness to positional notation; this card does not claim that its engraver invented zero.

A large terrace excavated at M.90 measures about 47 by 15 meters and stands roughly 2.1 meters high. Radiocarbon evidence places its construction around the middle of the sixth to middle of the seventh century. Researchers propose that it relates to the royal audience hall described in Chinese records; that identification remains an interpretation.

Researchers compared the thickness and chemical composition of bricks from 59 structures. The results revealed several construction groups and a more complicated building sequence than a single royal project. Ancient builders added, repaired and changed things. A monument can hold the history of many work crews rather than one grand opening day.

Modern Cambodian and Japanese researchers have combined local residents’ knowledge, field surveys and airborne laser mapping. Small mounds can conceal collapsed brick buildings, while subtle earthworks reveal channels and routes. The surviving temples are the most visible part of a much larger inhabited landscape, and research continues to recover its less spectacular spaces.

ending.text: Chenla has no securely demonstrated single collapse matching the map’s endpoint of 900. Political organization changed as Angkorian power emerged in the ninth century. Earlier temples remained in use and received later alterations. Khmer communities, language and craftsmanship continued; the end of this atlas label is not the disappearance of a people.
